stem: A 50 year old patient presents with 40% TBSA burns and a body weight of 70. Calculate the total fluid that should be given in the first 24 hours using parklands formula?
expl: Parkland = 4 × 70 kg × 40% = 11,200 ml in 24 h (half in the first 8 h).

stem: A patient presents to the ER with 9% second degree burns on the face and the hand. He is a known case of asthma and was coughing during initial stabilization. Which of the following is an indication for transfer to a burn center?

opts.t: Burns of the face and hand

expl: Burns of the face, hands, feet or genitalia are a referral criterion regardless of size; 9% second-degree is below the 20% threshold.

why.C: Coughing in a known asthmatic isn't a criterion (unless inhalation injury is suspected).

stem: A patient presents with 20% TBSA full thickness burns involving the extremities. Which of the following is the management?

opts.t: Surgical excision and grafting within 72 hours
Surgical excision and grafting after 2 weeks

expl: Full-thickness burns don't heal → early excision and grafting (within ~72 h) reduces infection, sepsis, stay and scarring.

why.C: Dressings alone can't heal full-thickness skin.

stem: A 35-year-old man with 40% body surface area burns was admitted to the ICU. He was intubated for airway protection, a central venous catheter was inserted, and he was started on total parenteral nutrition. After one week, he developed high-grade fever and leukocytosis. What is the most common ICU infection in burn patients?
expl: An intubated ICU patient's commonest infection is ventilator-associated pneumonia (the slides: most common surgical infection in ICU).

why.B: CLABSI is common but less than VAP.

stem: A 30-year-old man suffers an electrical shock at work. He is hemodynamically stable but complains of dark urine. Urinalysis shows hematuria, and serum tests reveal elevated creatine kinase. What is the most appropriate initial management?

opts.t: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and urine monitoring

expl: Electrical injury with dark urine and high CK = rhabdomyolysis → aggressive IV fluids targeting high urine output to protect the kidneys.

why.C: Diuretics alone without volume worsen injury.

stem: A 35-year-old woman sustains burns to her face and neck. She is hemodynamically stable, with no other injuries or comorbidities. Which of the following is an indication for transfer to a specialized burn center?

opts.t: Burns involving the face or neck

expl: Face/neck burns → burn centre (airway, cosmesis, function), even if small and stable.

stem: A patient who had an electric shock presented with dark urine. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Electrical injury damages muscle → myoglobin release → dark (tea-coloured) urine = rhabdomyolysis (→ AKI).

why.A: ATN is the consequence, not the cause of dark urine.

stem: A 67 year-old man, brought to ED after entrapment in a house fire, sustained 35% second degree burn. His blood tests showed potassium of 7.1 mEq/dl. Which of the following is appropriate treatment?
expl: 441 key: calcium gluconate — K⁺ 7.1 in a burn patient is life-threatening; protect the heart first. (The 438 version of the same question keyed insulin + dextrose.)

why.D: D5W without insulin doesn't lower K⁺.

stem: What is the Parkland formula?
expl: Parkland = 4 ml × weight (kg) × %TBSA burned (partial + full thickness).

stem: In a burn patient, what is the first step in management?
expl: ABCDE — airway first (inhalation injury can obstruct it quickly).

stem: A patient with electric shock presents to the ER. What is the primary complication that must be addressed immediately?
expl: High-voltage injury destroys muscle → rhabdomyolysis → myoglobinuric AKI → aggressive fluids (urine output 1–1.5 mL/kg/h) ± alkalinization; also cardiac monitoring.

why.A: Hypovolaemia is part of it, but rhabdomyolysis/AKI is the key electrical complication.

stem: burn patient with white leathery skin with loss of sensation and loss of capillary refill what degree is this?
expl: White/leathery, insensate, no capillary refill = full-thickness (third-degree).

stem: which of the following requires transfer to burn center :

opts.t: Third degree burn with less than (10% or 20 %

expl: Chemical burns are a referral criterion. A 2-cm second-degree burn isn't; the third-degree option is unclear in the recall.

why.C: Any third-degree burn is a criterion too — the recall was uncertain, and the key chose chemical burn.

stem: A 35-year-old male came to the emergency department, complaining of a burn in his left arm, he stated that he was cooking with hot oil, the burn was red, painless and had blisters, what degree is this burn?
expl: Keyed 2nd degree: blisters mean a partial-thickness (second-degree) burn; "painless" suggests deep partial thickness (nerve endings damaged).

why.B: Third-degree burns don't blister and are leathery.

stem: 30 YO male was transported to your burn centre suffering from facial, neck and chest burns due to explosion what will you do?

opts.t: Observe and when he gets worse you intubate

expl: Facial/neck burns from an explosion = high risk of inhalation injury and airway oedema → early intubation before swelling makes it impossible.

stem: A case of a burned patient and asks about the type of fluid appropriate for his resuscitation ?
srcNote: (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients)
expl: Burn resuscitation uses Ringer's lactate (Parkland).

why.B: Colloid/plasma isn't used in the first 24 h.

stem: What is the correct principle in the resuscitation of a burn patient? (similar phrasing to the exam Q)

opts.t: Ringer's lactate based on Parkland's only

srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: Burn resuscitation = Ringer's lactate by the Parkland formula PLUS normal maintenance (especially in children, who also need dextrose maintenance). The source had no key.

why.C: Parkland alone omits maintenance (important in children).

stem: a 33 years old man presented to emergency with burn and you are suspecting Second degree burn, What is the most diagnostic clinical feature for it?

opts.t: Loss of pain or painless burn

expl: Blistering is the hallmark of second-degree (partial-thickness) burns.

why.A: Blanching occurs in superficial burns too.

stem: A patient presented with a burn on his hand, he states that he was working on his car when he spilled hot antifreeze on his hand. The burn looks red, painful with blisters. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Soak hand in cold water for 20 minutes
Sterile dressing and keep hand below?

expl: Hand burns (function) → refer to a burn specialist, even when small.

why.B: Cooling is first aid immediately after injury, not the management now.
why.C: Part of care but not the key step.

stem: A 67 y/o man, brought to ED after entrapment in a house fire, he sustained 35% second degree burn. His blood tests showed potassium of 7.1 mEq/dl. Which of the following is appropriate treatment?

opts.t: Infusion of 5% dextrose 1 L over 4 hours

srcNote: (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients)
expl: 438 key: insulin + dextrose — drives K⁺ into cells. (The 441 version keyed calcium gluconate; give calcium first if there are ECG changes.)

why.B: Salbutamol 20 mg IV isn't the standard route/dose (it's nebulized).
why.C: Keyed in the 441 version; first if ECG changes.

stem: which of the following represents the coagulation zone of burns?
expl: The zone of coagulation is irreversibly necrotic tissue — corresponds to full-thickness (third-degree) injury.

why.B: Deep partial is closer to the stasis zone.

stem: A 32-year-old healthy male who weighs 70 kg sustained a flame burn in a closed room after his bed caught fire from an electrical circuit malfunction. He burned his right lower extremity, half of his anterior trunk and his head and neck area with evidence of significant facial hair burn. His burn occurred at 2:00pm to the emergency at 5:00pm. Clinically his burns were of deep second degree, and third degrees only. What is the TBSA (Total body surface area), burn of this patient?
srcNote: (Burns) Source note (437 A Q16): “Question was deleted (Burns)”. That version lists 27%, 45%, 70% and 61%; the retained 438 A version is reproduced above.
expl: Right lower limb 18% + half of anterior trunk 9% + head and neck 9% = 36%.

stem: A 3 year old child weighs 13 kg, sustained a 25% TBSA burn of second and third degree. According to the parkland formula he received 1300 ml of ringer lactate intravenously in the first 24 hours, then the child was found unconscious the next day. What is the most likely cause?

opts.t: Brain edema due to fluid overload

srcNote: (Burns) Limited hepatic glycogen storage in children makes them high risk for hypoglycemia in the first 24h following a burn
expl: Children have small glycogen stores; a burned child given RL without dextrose maintenance can become hypoglycemic within 24 h → unconscious. 1300 ml for 13 kg × 25% = exactly Parkland, so not overload.

stem: Caloric intake requirement in burn patients:
srcNote: , calculate it as per curreri formula 25kcal/kg + 40kcal/TBSA% (if pediatric 60kcal/kg) (Burns)
expl: Keyed 70 (odd recall). The Curreri formula is 25 kcal/kg + 40 kcal per %TBSA (the doctor corrected it to 20 kcal/kg); children 60 kcal/kg. None of the options matches exactly — the source key is A.

why.B: 40 kcal is the per-%TBSA part of Curreri.

stem: A person had a flame in a closed space because of electricity. After stabilizing the patient and giving IVF ,What is the most important next step?
expl: After airway and fluids, a burn patient from a closed-space fire needs assessment of circumferential burns for compartment syndrome/escharotomy (life/limb-threatening) before wound care.

stem: A 26 year old male sustained a 35% TBSA third degree burn. He is planned for multiple debridement and skin grafting procedures. The problem that there is no enough donor skin. What is the best technique to ensure that the donor skin available will be enough for the procedure?
expl: Meshing makes slits in a split-thickness graft so it can be expanded (e.g. 1.5:1 to 3:1) to cover a larger area when donor sites are limited. Allografts, xenografts and dermal substitutes are temporary covers.

why.D: Needs a graft on top later; doesn't increase donor skin.

stem: 18 y\o man sustained chemical burn due hydrofluoric acid involving the anterior surface of the trunk and lower limbs. Which of the following is the most important initial step in the management of chemical injury?

opts.t: Intravenous fluid resuscitation using parkland formula

expl: Chemical burns → remove the agent: copious water irrigation (≥ 30 min). For hydrofluoric acid add calcium gluconate and monitor calcium/ECG.

why.A: Fluids if the TBSA is large, after decontamination.

stem: A 37 y/o male sustained a 60% body surface area burn. The burn involved the right lower extremity, half of the anterior trunk and his head and neck area. All were of second and third degree burns. The patient was given initial resuscitation and was connected to a Foley catheter to monitor his urine output. Patient became oliguric thereafter. What is the most probable cause of oliguria in this patient?

opts.t: Getting NS IV fluid instead of ringer lactate
Urethral injury caused by foley catheter
Injury to the kidney (nephrons) from muscles' burn

srcNote: ? Source note (438 F Q42): Answer: C?
expl: Keyed (with "?" in the source): oliguria from myoglobin-induced kidney injury after deep burns involving muscle. Under-resuscitation is the commonest cause of oliguria, so increase fluids first.

why.A: NS vs RL doesn't cause oliguria.
why.B: Urethral injury from a catheter is unlikely.

stem: A3-vear-old child weighs 13kg, sustained a 25% (BSA) Total body surface area burn of second and third degree. According to the Parkland formula he received 1300 ml of ringer lactate intravenously in the first 24hours, then the child was found unconscious the next day. What is the most likely cause?

opts.t: Brain edema due to fluid overload

srcNote: Source note (435 A Q49 (p. 140)): ANSWER: D (Burn) (idk, repeated question, maybe B)
expl: 4 × 13 × 25 = 1300 mL (Parkland only). Children < 30 kg also need dextrose-containing maintenance fluid because of small glycogen stores — without it they become hypoglycaemic. One version keyed brain oedema.

why.C: Possible, but hypoglycaemia explains unconsciousness best.

stem: A 50-year-old male patient had a third degree burn and a second degree circumferential burn, which of the following is a poor prognostic indicator in his case?
expl: Carbonaceous sputum = inhalation injury → the strongest poor prognostic factor (with age and TBSA); circumferential burns are a treatable complication.

stem: Patient with electrical burn, and fell from 3m height, he is unconscious. entry point is right shoulder, exit point left shoulder. What is the next step?
expl: Unconscious patient (electrical injury + fall) cannot protect the airway → intubation (with C-spine protection) first; cardiac monitoring follows.

stem: A 43-year old man, who weighs 70 kg is brought to emergency department with first degree burns to the face, circumferential second degree burns to both lower limbs and third degree burns to the anterior chest and abdomen. Which of the following is the estimated total volume of fluid needed for resuscitation over the first 24 hours (using the Parkland formula)?
srcNote: Source note (435 A Q7 (p. 128)): Answer: a (burns) (Parklands formula: 4ml x weight (kg) x %BSA “excluding 1st degree burns”)
expl: First-degree face burns aren't counted. Circumferential both legs (2 × 18 = 36%) + anterior chest and abdomen (18%) = 54%. 4 × 70 × 54 = 15,120 mL of Ringer's lactate.

why.C: Includes the face — first-degree burns don't count.

stem: A 70kg male patient presented with an electric burn involved the right lower extremity, half of the anterior trunk and his head and neck area. All were of second and third degree burns. The burn happened at 2 am and the patient presented to the ER at 5 am. Calculate his fluid requirements per hour in the first 8 hours?
expl: Burn = right leg 18% + half anterior trunk 9% + head/neck 9% = 36%. Parkland: 4 × 70 × 36 = 10,080 ml; half = 5,040 ml in the first 8 h → 630 ml/h (keyed). Strictly, the first-8-h volume is counted from the time of burn, so with a 3-h delay it would be given over 5 h (~1,008 ml/h).

why.C: Close to the delay-adjusted rate, but not keyed.

stem: 40y.o pt weight 70kg he had multiple burns and circumferential right upper limb. What is the management of this limb?

opts.t: Frequent monitoring and Calculate compartment pressure

expl: Circumferential limb burn with (risk of) compartment syndrome → escharotomy (release the eschar).

stem: A 2- year old baby boy was seen in the emergency department with burn to his hands and chest. Which of the following is the most common type of burn in the pediatric population?
expl: Scalds (hot liquids) are the commonest burns in children.

stem: What is the most diagnostic clinical feature for second degree burn?

opts.t: Loss of pain or painless burn

expl: Blistering is the most characteristic sign of second-degree (partial-thickness) burns.

stem: 40 y/o patient weight 70kg he had multiple burns and circumferential right upper limb. What is the management of his right upper limb?
expl: A circumferential upper-limb burn needs escharotomy (fasciotomy only if compartment syndrome persists after escharotomy, or electrical/crush injuries).

why.C: Fasciotomy is for deep muscle compartment syndrome.

stem: Patient in ER after electrical injury. He was unconscious. What is the initial step in management?
expl: An unconscious patient can't protect the airway → intubation first; ECG monitoring after.

stem: A 43 y\o man, who weighs 70 Kg, brought to the emergency department with first degree burn to the face, circumferential second degree burn to both lower limbs and third degree burn to the anterior chest and abdomen. Which of the following is the estimated total volume of fluid needed to resuscitation over the first 24 hours ?
srcNote: (Burn) (Parklands formula: 4ml x weight (kg) x %BSA “excluding 1st degree burns”)
expl: Exclude 1st-degree (face). 2nd-degree both legs circumferential = 36%, 3rd-degree anterior chest + abdomen = 18% → 54%. 4 × 70 × 54 = 15,120 ml RL.

stem: A 30-year-old man who repairs electrical lines for a utility company is brought to the emergency department for the treatment of an electrical injury to the right upper extremity. Examination shows limited full-thickness burns of the flexor creases of the palm, wrist, and elbow. Doppler flowmetry shows patent palmar arch pulses. Passive motion of the fingers produces severe pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
expl: Keyed fasciotomy: high-voltage injury destroys deep muscle (skin burns underestimate it) → compartment syndrome → fasciotomy (± debridement), even with palpable pulses.

stem: An otherwise healthy 32-year-old man who has a severe burn scar at the elbow. undergoes contracture release. Which of the following reconstructive methods is most likely to result in recurrent contracture?
expl: Split-thickness grafts have little dermis and contract most (secondary contraction), so contracture recurs. Flaps bring their own tissue and resist contraction.

stem: What’s the TBSA % in a patient w third degree burn of the face, third degree circumferential burn of right leg and thigh and abdomen + thorax?
expl: Keyed 36%: anterior trunk (18%) + whole right lower limb (18%) — this recall appears to be a version of the question where the face/arms were first-degree (not counted). If the face were truly third-degree it would add ~4.5–9%.

stem: Old male pt. brought to the hospital suffering from a burn. He was referred to the burn unit late. What is the most important factor deciding the prognosis?
expl: Age is a major prognostic factor (Baux score = age + %TBSA); late referral matters less.

stem: A man with first degree burns to arms, second degree to anterior thorax and abdomen and circumferential to the right lower leg and thigh. Which one of the following is the correct estimation of the burnt body surface area to calculate fluid replacement?
expl: First-degree arm burns aren't counted. Anterior thorax + abdomen = 18%; circumferential right lower limb = 18% → 36%.

stem: female 30 years of age got 2nd and 3rd degree burns in the right upper arm, circumferential she lives in a small town, the hospital in the small town is fully equipped with basic burn tools what would be the reason for referral to a bigger hospital?
expl: Circumferential deep burns risk compartment syndrome and need escharotomy/specialist care → referral criterion.

stem: 42 y/o man brought to emergency department as burn victim. On examination he was found to have bilateral upper extremity 2nd and 3rd degree burn, anterior surface of lower extremity 2nd degree burn.What is the % of burn?
expl: Keyed 27%: both upper limbs (2 × 9 = 18%) + the anterior surface of one lower limb (9%) = 27%.

stem: A 45 y/o patient admitted to burn unit 3 weeks ago with 40% full thickness burn referred surgery with history of vomiting large amount of fresh blood.Which of the following is the most likely source of the bleeding?
srcNote: ( Burns ) Curling's ulcer is an acute gastric erosion resulting as a complication from severe burns when reduced plasma volume leads to ischemia and cell necrosis (sloughing) of the gastric mucosa.
expl: Curling's ulcer = acute stress ulceration of the stomach/duodenum after major burns (hypovolaemia → mucosal ischaemia). Prevent with early enteral feeding and acid suppression.

why.D: Cushing's ulcer follows head/CNS injury (vagal overstimulation → high acid).

stem: An 18 y/o man with sustained chemical burning involving the anterior surface of the trunk and lower limbs. Which of the following is the most important initial step in the management?
expl: Chemical burns → first remove the agent by copious water irrigation (then fluids, tetanus).

stem: What is the indication of meshing? (in graft)

opts.t: In case of small donor area.

srcNote: Skin graft meshing: The mesh incisions allow the graft to be expanded to cover large defects when donor sites are limited.
expl: Meshing lets a graft be expanded so less donor skin covers a larger area — for large burns with limited donor sites.

why.B: Also related, but the key is A.

stem: Which one of the following is a sign of full thickness (3rd degree) burn?
expl: Thrombosed (coagulated) superficial veins visible through the burn = full-thickness burn.

stem: Marjolijn ulcer “incomplete question” probably they meant what type of cancer it’s most likely associated with
expl: Long-standing scars/ulcers undergo malignant change to SCC.
ansText: SCC — a Marjolin ulcer is an aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound or burn scar.

stem: 15 years old female with scaled burn involving her face and upper trunk, what is the Best management:

opts.t: ABC, if stable, ask her to go home
IV fluid then admission to burn unit
Depends on last tetanus toxoid vaccine date.

expl: Facial burn (with trunk) = referral criterion → IV fluids and admission to a burn unit (airway/cosmetic site).

stem: indication for admission in burn unit:
expl: Smoke/inhalation injury → admit to the burn unit (airway risk).

why.A: Feet are a referral site, but the key is smoke inhalation.

stem: Clue for inhalation injury:
srcNote: , I think they mean presence of burned hair in nostrils, it’s termed Singed vibrissae (Burns)
expl: Singed nasal hair (vibrissae), facial burns, soot and closed-space fire suggest inhalation injury.

stem: Sulphuric acid “incomplete Q”
srcNote: Source key was C; corrected — see explanation. , previous year comment on this Q as “the doctor said in the lecture irrigate for one hour” It is an acid, B is correct
expl: Acid burns are treated by prolonged copious irrigation (the doctor said about one hour; the source comment says B is correct). An ECG matters for hydrofluoric acid or electrical injury, not sulphuric acid.

why.C: Not the key step for sulphuric acid.

stem: What is the immediate management of inhalation injury?

opts.t: immediate management is ABC and intubation

ansText: ABC with early (prophylactic) intubation before airway oedema develops, and 100% oxygen (carbon monoxide).

stem: 3 years old boy 13 kg get burned with 25% TBSA according to parkland formula he was given ringer lactate 1300 ml. Next day patient collapsed. What is the cause of this case?
expl: Parkland alone (4 × 13 × 25 = 1300 mL) gives no glucose; young children need dextrose maintenance → hypoglycaemia.

stem: Patient presented with 55% TBSA needed to donor graft and we need to insure enough donor skin, which of the following modalities can be used?
srcNote: Practical Procedures and Investigation of Surgical Patients
expl: Meshing expands a split-thickness autograft (e.g. 1:1.5–1:3) so limited donor skin covers large burns. Allografts/xenografts are temporary.
